In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''reflexive sheaf''' is a [[coherent sheaf]] that is isomorphic to its second dual (as a [[sheaf of modules]]) via the canonical map. The second dual of a coherent sheaf is called the '''reflexive hull''' of the sheaf. A basic example of a reflexive sheaf is a [[locally free sheaf]] of finite rank. The notion is important both in [[scheme theory]] and [[complex algebraic geometry]].

For the theory of reflexive sheaves, one works over an [[Integral domain|integral]] [[Noetherian scheme|noetherian]] [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]].

A reflexive sheaf is torsion-free. The dual of a coherent sheaf is reflexive.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1980|loc=Corollary 1.2.}}</ref> Usually, the product of reflexive sheaves is defined as the reflexive hull of their tensor products (so the result is reflexive).

A coherent sheaf ''F'' is said to be "normal" in the sense of Barth if the restriction <math>F(U) \to F(U - Y)</math> is bijective for every open subset ''U'' and a closed subset ''Y'' of ''U'' of codimension at least 2. With this terminology, a coherent sheaf on an integral [[normal scheme]] is reflexive if and only if it is [[torsion-free sheaf|torsion-free]] and normal in the sense of Barth.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1980|loc=Proposition 1.6.}}</ref> A reflexive sheaf of rank one on an integral [[locally factorial scheme|locally factorial]] scheme is invertible.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1980|loc=Proposition 1.9.}}</ref>

A '''divisorial sheaf''' on a scheme ''X'' is a rank-one reflexive sheaf that is locally free at the generic points of the [[conductor (algebraic geometry)|conductor]] ''D''<sub>''X''</sub> of ''X''.<ref>{{harvnb|Kollár|loc=Ch. 3, § 1.}}</ref> For example, a [[canonical sheaf]] ([[dualizing sheaf]]) on a normal projective variety is a divisorial sheaf.
